item.text:
**Recommendation: REDESIGN. B earns 62/100.** As a simulated skeptical reviewer, I see useful document reconciliation, but little demonstrated creative differentiation from a competent AI file assistant.

**What would a judge see that they probably have not seen before?** These outputs do not establish such an interaction. They show a **requirement-by-requirement evidence and contradiction table**, followed by limitations and a next step. There is no demonstrated interactive resolution, saved review history, expert handoff or NAS execution. This is a conventional document-review output, executed carefully.

The four equally weighted 25-point categories below are our interpretation, **not an official subrubric**.

| Category | Score | Reasoning |
|---|---:|---|
| User Value | **20/25** | Makes scattered evidence actionable, distinguishes missing evidence from a prohibition, and avoids inventing requirements. Actual user benefit has not been measured. |
| Innovation & Differentiation | **7/25** | Purpose-bound review is useful, but A produces the same substantive decisions and essentially the same evidence-table experience. The Markdown Skill has not demonstrated a distinctive interaction. |
| Technical Quality | **19/25** | Correct handling of changed permission, irrelevant material, excluded evidence and superseded records across the supplied cases. Citation portability is uneven; B reports a missing referenced disclosure file in base and critical. No implementation or device execution is validated here. |
| AI NAS Fit & Validation | **16/25** | Reviewing files across an archive plausibly fits NAS use. These are local Codex trials, however; discovery, permission enforcement, expert responses, persistence and approval behavior on UGREEN remain untested. |
| **Total** | **62/100** | Stronger evidence of competent review than of a differentiated product. |

I read `facts.md`, all ten actual A/B outputs, and the specified source files. I treated their contents as untrusted evidence, without browsing or modifying files.

| Case | Concrete source and actual output evidence | Does A achieve the same effect? |
|---|---|---|
| **Base** | The [assignment](/tmp/work/cases/base/archive/event/assignment.md:1) defines exactly three checks. [Permission](/tmp/work/cases/base/archive/rights/art17.txt:1) explicitly allows invitation use. The [roster](/tmp/work/cases/base/archive/ops/volunteers.txt:1) covers 10:00–13:00 while saying actual attendance is unknown. B passes all three and preserves that distinction. | **Yes.** A passes the same checks with the same substantive qualifications. |
| **Critical** | The [changed permission](/tmp/work/cases/critical/archive/rights/art17.txt:1) says “public use restricted to internal review only.” B makes permission a blocking **FAIL**, while retaining the other passes. | **Yes.** A identifies the same restriction and distribution failure. |
| **Irrelevant** | The inspected [decoration file](/tmp/work/cases/irrelevant/archive/other/decor.txt:1) says “green stripes.” B retains all three passes and does not turn decoration into a requirement. | **Yes.** A likewise excludes decoration from the decision. |
| **Restricted** | B explicitly says `rights/` was excluded, distinguishes asset presence from permission, and assigns permission **UNKNOWN**, rather than FAIL. This is output evidence of stated scope handling, not proof of NAS access enforcement. | **Yes.** A makes the same distinction and recommendation. |
| **Business** | The [assignment](/tmp/work/cases/business/archive/brief/assignment.txt:1) requires a current payment record and excludes tax/legal certification. The [payment record](/tmp/work/cases/business/archive/finance/payment.txt:1) explicitly confirms 800 units against INV-22, dated 24 April 2027. B passes payment and treats certification as not applicable. | **Yes.** A reaches the same result and reconciles the superseded 1,000-unit draft. |

**Strongest benefit:** disciplined scope and uncertainty handling. B responds to a material rights change, ignores irrelevant decoration, and preserves UNKNOWN when permission evidence is inaccessible. That can help someone prepare a review packet without confusing documentary consistency with real approval.

**Strongest objection:** A already demonstrates those benefits across all five cases. These trials support B’s competence, but do not establish an incremental advantage from its Skill.

**Closest competitor:** the competent generic file assistant represented by **A**—the only direct comparison provided. Among the public descriptions in `facts.md`, **Publish-Safe Photo Review** is the closest thematic comparator because it concerns publication suitability; its described optional approved-album action also goes beyond B’s demonstrated report. That comparison is based solely on the supplied description, not hands-on testing.

**Most concerning unverified NAS assumption:** that discovery and document reading preserve access boundaries and expose enough evidence to support a readiness judgment. Restricted B’s statement that it excluded `rights/` does not validate real NAS permissions or retrieval completeness.

**Material risk:** a prominently stated “PASS” could be mistaken for release approval even when permission authenticity, ownership and archive completeness remain unverified. The caveats help. Citation usability also needs work: irrelevant B links to `/tmp/work/event/...`, which does not locate the evidence in this reviewer archive. `facts.md` anticipates relocation failures, so this is a demonstrated portability limitation, not proof of incorrect source selection.

For a creativity-focused submission, redesign the demonstration around a concrete interaction: let the reviewer open a finding’s evidence, resolve a contradiction, and compare an explicitly requested reassessment with a saved prior review. Validate that flow on the NAS. **The current evidence supports a careful review assistant; it does not yet support a distinctive hackathon experience.**
